# Toronto Rent Increase Notice: Practical Next Steps

Your notice says the rent would rise **8% on 2026-09-01**, and your lease ends **2026-08-31**. Since you’ve lived there **14 months**, the key questions are whether the unit is subject to Ontario rent control, whether the increase follows the required notice rules, and whether the timing matches the end of your lease.

## What to Review Before You Reply

- **Unit type and first occupancy date**
  - Confirm whether the home is a rental unit covered by Ontario rent rules.
  - Check whether the unit was first occupied for residential use before **2018-11-15**; that can affect whether an annual guideline cap applies.

- **Notice timing and format**
  - Review whether you received the notice on the proper form and with enough notice before the effective date.
  - Check whether the increase is being treated as a lease renewal change, a guideline increase, or an above-guideline request.

- **Lease end date vs. increase date**
  - Your lease ends **2026-08-31**, so the landlord may be linking a new term to the new rent.
  - Confirm whether you are being asked to sign a new lease, stay month-to-month, or accept a rent adjustment tied to a renewal.

- **Amount of increase**
  - An **8%** increase is above Ontario’s annual guideline for many rent-controlled units, so it is worth asking for the basis of the increase.
  - If the unit is exempt from rent control, the cap may not apply in the same way, but notice and lease terms still matter.

- **Any extra charges**
  - Check whether the notice changes only base rent or also adds parking, storage, utilities, or other fees.

## Documents and Details to Gather

- Current lease and any renewal drafts
- The rent increase notice or email
- Proof of when you first moved in
- Rent payment records for the last 14 months
- Any messages about repairs, previous increases, or lease changes
- Photos or notes if the unit’s condition is relevant to your decision
- A copy of the building address, unit number, and landlord/property manager contact details
- Any written promises about included services, parking, or utilities

## Practical Checklist for Your Reply

- Verify the **effective date** and whether it matches the required notice period
- Ask whether the **8%** is:
  - a guideline increase,
  - an above-guideline request,
  - or a new lease price after expiry
- Ask if the unit is considered **rent-controlled** or **exempt**
- Ask for the increase **in writing** with the legal basis and calculation
- Confirm whether you need to sign anything before **2026-08-31**
- Keep paying the current rent unless you receive clear written instructions that are valid and you choose to accept the change
- Save every email, text, and notice in one folder

## Polite Message Template to Ask for Clarification

Subject: Request for clarification on rent increase notice

Hello [Landlord/Property Manager Name],

Thank you for sending the notice regarding the rent change effective 2026-09-01.

Before I respond, I’d like to confirm a few details:
- Is the unit subject to Ontario rent control?
- Is the 8% increase based on a guideline increase, a lease renewal amount, or another reason?
- Could you please confirm the notice period and provide the increase in writing with the calculation used?
- Will this change apply only to base rent, or are any other charges changing as well?

My current lease ends on 2026-08-31, so I want to make sure I understand the terms clearly before making any decision.

Thank you for your help.

Kind regards,
[Your Name]
[Unit Number]

## Quick Actions

Action: [Button: Review Ontario rules](https://www.ontario.ca/page/residential-rent-increases)
Action: [Button: Tenant support info](https://www.torontotenants.org/)
Action: [Button: Lease and notice checklist](https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/)

## Sources

- Ontario rent increases: https://www.ontario.ca/page/residential-rent-increases
- Landlord and Tenant Board: https://tribunalsontario.ca/ltb/
- Toronto tenants resource: https://www.torontotenants.org/
